We defined refugia as isolated 1 km × 1 km grid cells with multiple Arctic-alpine plant species occurrences outside their main distribution area and assessed the main environmental factors underlying their distribution and richness using cross-validated boosted regression tree modelling. results.title: Comparing Spatial and Multilevel Regression Models for ...
results.content: This research systematically compares model estimations and predictions for binary outcomes between (distance- and lattice-based) spatial and the standard multilevel models in the presence of both within- and between-neighborhood correlations, through simulations. By systematically comparing model performance in estimation and prediction between spatial and the standard multilevel models in the presence of both within- and between-neighborhood correlations through simulation analyses, this study informs researchers about making cautious model choices whenever spatial information is available, in addition to standard multilevel data structures. The simulation analysis here compares spatial and the standard multilevel models with respect to parameter estimation and prediction in the presence of both within- and between-neighborhood correlations. Four models were fitted to each simulated data set and compared, including a _standard multilevel model_ that adjusts for within-neighborhood correlation, a _pure spatial model_ that adjusts for distance-based between-neighborhood correlation but ignores within-neighborhood correlation, and two hybrid models that adjust for both within- and between-neighborhood correlations. Moreover, in the case of fully out-of-sample cross validation, the coefficient estimate for the neighborhood-level predictor (γ 1) is relatively less biased in the standard multilevel and hybrid CAR models than that in the pure and hybrid spatial models, although the four models do not differ substantially as measured by CR and MSE. Open in a new tab Posterior means of neighborhood effects from the standard multilevel model (top) and that of spatial effects from the hybrid spatial model (bottom) fitted to the child mortality data of 1880 Newark, NJ. Open in a new tab Estimates of spatial correlation from distance-based (exponential) pure and hybrid spatial logit models fitted to the child mortality data of 1880 Newark, NJ The standard multilevel regressions which are widely used in neighborhood research typically ignore potential between-neighborhood correlation due to underlying spatial processes, and hence are subject to biased statistical inference. Through systematic comparisons of model estimations and predictions for binary outcomes using both simulation and empirical data, this study sheds new light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of spatial models as compared to the standard multilevel model, and is informative for future research on neighborhood and spatial effects. First, the standard multilevel and spatial models have similar performance with respect to estimating parameters of fixed effects as well as predicting new observations within existing neighborhoods.

results.title: A New Approach to Identifying Crash Hotspot Intersections (CHIs) Using Spatial Weights Matrices
results.content: In this paper we develop a new approach to directly detect crash hotspot intersections (CHIs) using two customized spatial weights matrices, which are the inverse network distance-band spatial weights matrix of intersections (INDSWMI) and the k-nearest distance-band spatial weights matrix between crash and intersection (KDSWMCI). crash hotspot intersections (CHIs); road network; traffic crash; spatial weights matrix (SWM); Getis–Ord Gi\*; hotspot analysis; Intersection Prediction Accuracy Index (IPAI). To solve these issues, first, we take intersections instead of crashes as the research object, which can directly identify CHIs. Second, the inverse network distance-band spatial weights matrix of intersections (INDSWMI) and the k-nearest distance-band spatial weights matrix between crash and intersection (KDSWMCI) are developed and applied to hotspot analysis to improve the accuracy of the results of CHI identification. The main tasks of this study include (a) creating the INDSWMI with respect to road network restraints; (b) building the KDSWMCI based on the k-nearest neighbors and distance-bands by obtaining the adjacency crashes and the number of crashes at each intersection; (c) testing the Intersection Prediction Accuracy Index (IPAI) of the proposed approach and identifying the CHIs to help safety researchers develop safety strategies to reduce crashes. This paper presents a three-step approach to directly identifying crash hotspot intersections (CHIs) by using (1) construction of the inverse network distance-band spatial weights matrix of intersection (INDSWMI), (2) construction of the k-nearest distance-band spatial weights matrix between crash and intersection (KDSWMCI), and (3) intersection hotspot analysis (IHA). results.title: Spatial summation of thermal sensitivity is limited to small areas: Comparisons of the forehead, forearm, abdomen, and foot - ScienceDirect
results.content: The purpose of the present study was to examine if spatial summation in thermal sensitivity exists when stimulating areas larger than about 1% of body surface area (BSA) (approximately 200 cm2). Fifteen young males participated in this study and we measured their warmth and hot sensation thresholds on the four body regions (the forehead, forearm, abdomen, and instep) using the three sizes of radiant film heaters (10 × 10, 15 × 15, and 20 × 20 cm2 heating film area). Early studies based on classical methodologies reported that human sensitivity was varied according to exposed stimulus area sizes: the larger the surface area exposed to a heat source, the lower the thermal thresholds (Defrin et al., 2009; Green and Zaharchuk, 2001; Pertovaara et al., 1996; Price et al., 1989). Studies above often mentioned the term of a spatial summation, which is the synaptic integration of input signals from several and distributed presynaptic neurons (Etherington et al., 2010) and is related to the size of areas or the number of neurons stimulated. As addressed above, however, most previous studies reported the effects of thermal probes stimulating very small areas (e.g., 1–16 cm2), and a small fraction of the human body surface area (<0.1%) (Lee et al., 2008). In this regard, we investigated whether any spatial summation of thermal sensitivity exists when increasing the area stimulated by radiant heat from 100–400 cm2. Our hypothesis was that spatial summation of thermal sensitivity, which has been well documented by previous studies, would not exist in large areas of approximately 200–400 cm2 on all the four body regions. The novel finding of the present study was that the spatial summation was not found in areas much larger than 225 cm2, even though larger heating areas induced lower thermal thresholds (higher thermal sensitivity) in the range of 100–225 cm2. We found that the spatial summation in thermal sensitivity was not found in areas larger than 225 cm2 (approximately, 1–1.5%BSA) even though larger heating areas induced lower thermal thresholds (higher thermal sensitivity) in smaller areas below the 225 cm2. That is, spatial summation in thermal sensitivity exists in small areas but the effect becomes insignificant once the stimulus area exceeds a certain size (> approximately 1–1.5%BSA).
